stages.name: Derby to Newark
stages.note: Down the Trent through Long Eaton and Nottingham

stages.name: Newark to Lincoln
stages.note: North with the Trent to the Great Army camp at Torksey, then the Fossdyke

stages.name: Lincoln to Barton-upon-Humber
stages.note: North along Ermine Street to the Humber

stages.name: Barton-upon-Humber to Howden
stages.note: Over the Humber Bridge, then west along the estuary

stages.name: Howden to York
stages.note: Up the Ouse through Selby to Jorvik

routes.name: Way of the Roses Cycle Route

sites.name: Derby
sites.text: One of the Five Boroughs of the Danelaw. Its name is Old Norse, Djúrabý, "deer farm". Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, took it back from the Danes in 917.

sites.name: Repton
sites.text: 13 km up the Trent from Derby, off the route. The Great Heathen Army wintered here in 873–874 and drove out the Mercian king; a Viking camp and burials have been excavated by the church.

sites.name: Nottingham
sites.text: Another of the Five Boroughs. The Great Heathen Army wintered here in 867–868. The route crosses the Trent at Trent Bridge.

sites.name: Torksey
sites.text: The Great Army's winter camp of 872–873, where the Fossdyke meets the Trent. Metal-detecting and excavation have found thousands of finds: hack silver, weights and lead gaming pieces.

sites.name: Fossdyke
sites.text: A canal joining the Trent at Torksey to the Witham at Lincoln, probably Roman and still navigable: the route follows its towpath into Lincoln.

sites.name: Lincoln
sites.text: One of the Five Boroughs, with a busy Viking-age mint. The route leaves north along Ermine Street, the Roman road to the Humber.

sites.name: Gainsborough
sites.text: Off the route, north of Torksey on the Trent. Sweyn Forkbeard, king of Denmark, made it his base when he conquered England in 1013 and died there in 1014.

sites.name: Barton-upon-Humber
sites.text: The old ferry town on the south bank of the Humber. St Peter's Church has an Anglo-Saxon tower from around the end of the 10th century.

sites.name: Humber
sites.text: The estuary the Great Army crossed on its way to York in 866. The route crosses it on the Humber Bridge.

sites.name: Selby
sites.text: A name of Old Norse origin, probably "willow farm", like many -by places along the route.

sites.name: Riccall
sites.text: Harald Hardrada's fleet came up the Ouse and landed here in September 1066, the last great Viking invasion of England.

sites.name: Fulford
sites.text: Harald Hardrada beat the northern earls here on 20 September 1066, five days before his defeat at Stamford Bridge.

sites.name: York
sites.text: Jorvik. The Great Heathen Army took it on 1 November 866, and it was the capital of a Viking kingdom until Eric Bloodaxe was driven out in 954.
